title: Phillies clinch wild card on final day after nearly historic collapse
dek: Philadelphia defeated Tampa Bay 7-1 on September 27 to secure the National League wild card berth, ending a week in which they nearly became the first team since 1903 to blow a four-game lead with five games remaining. The team that opened 9-19 and fired its manager in late April reached the postseason under Don Mattingly.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: The Phillies beat Tampa Bay 7-1 on the final day of the season to clinch the wild card after losing four consecutive games while Arizona won four straight, nearly erasing a four-game lead.
bottom_line: The Phillies' wild card matchup in the first round and Luzardo's readiness for playoff action following his late-season shoulder issues will shape their ability to advance beyond the postseason's opening round.
body:
The Philadelphia Phillies reached the postseason on September 27 by defeating the Tampa Bay Rays 7-1 in a must-win game on the final day of the regular season, securing the National League wild card berth after a week in which they came closer to historic failure than any team in 123 years of postseason baseball.
The Phillies held a four-game lead over Arizona with five games to play. According to MLB.com, no team since postseason play began in 1903 had blown such a lead with that many games remaining. Last week, the Phillies lost four consecutive games while the Diamondbacks won four in a row, narrowing what had been a comfortable margin to a single game before Sunday's clincher.
The 1964 Phillies, the franchise's most notorious collapse, blew a 6.5-game lead with 12 games to play, ceding the National League pennant to St. Louis. The 2026 team stopped short of that fate, though the trajectory and the tension were unmistakable. The Phillies opened 9-19, a record that cost manager Rob Thomson his job on April 28. Don Mattingly replaced him, and the team built its way back to contention through the summer before the September skid tested everything that recovery had promised.
The Phillies' offense, meanwhile, showed signs of life after going dormant during the losing streak. During the four losses, the Phillies scored just three runs total, including a 21-inning scoreless drought that marked their longest in 15 months.
Zack Wheeler took the mound on short rest. The Phillies had originally planned to skip his Sunday start and reserve him for Game 1 of the Wild Card Series on Tuesday, but changed course to use him in the clinch game. Wheeler allowed one run over six innings, and the Phillies scored early and often. Bryson Stott started cleanup for just the seventh time in his career and drove in a run with a two-out double in the first. J.T. Realmuto, snapping an 0-for-34 slump, doubled home a run in the second to extend the lead to 2-0. Kyle Schwarber's two-out double in the same inning scored two more to make it 4-0, per MLB.com. Schwarber's hit left his bat at 116.8 mph, his hardest-hit base hit of the season by 3.8 mph. Bryce Harper added a solo homer in the fifth, the team's first since Tuesday and Harper's first since September 12, according to the source.
Jesús Luzardo, sidelined since September 7 with inflammation in his left shoulder and making his first appearance against hitters on Sunday, retired the side on four pitches in the eighth. Alex McFarlane allowed two runs in the seventh, the only blemish on a day when the Phillies seized control and refused to relinquish it.
The clinch came on the 162nd and final day of the season, a margin that left no room for error and no tomorrow. The Phillies are now in the postseason; what unfolds next remains unwritten.
